title: Direct Memory Translation for Virtualized Clouds
problem: Virtual memory translation is a performance bottleneck in virtualized environments. On x86 architecture, nested translation requires sequential fetching of up to 24 page table entries, imposing severe overhead for memory-intensive workloads.
motivation: Reducing virtual memory translation overhead is critical for improving performance of memory-intensive applications in virtualized cloud environments.
method: DMT (Direct Memory Translation) stores page table entries—the mappings that tell the CPU where memory physically lives—in contiguous memory blocks called Translation Entry Areas (TEAs). Instead of searching through a hierarchy of page tables, the system maintains direct mappings from virtual addresses to these PTEs using dedicated CPU registers, organized per virtual memory region (VMA). When the guest OS and host cooperate, the guest's TEAs can be placed in physical memory, bypassing the virtualization layers that normally add overhead. This cuts translation lookups to one, two, or three memory accesses for native, virtualized, and nested virtualized systems respectively—compared to the original 24 sequential page table fetches.
key_novelty: Storing page table entries (memory-address mappings) in contiguous Translation Entry Areas and mapping them directly per memory region—instead of through nested hierarchy searches—enables nested virtualization without lookup overhead while maintaining x86 compatibility.
contributions: DMT hardware-software extension for x86 virtual memory with full backward compatibility
Translation Entry Areas (TEAs) abstraction for managed contiguous page table entry storage
Per-VMA direct mapping mechanism using dedicated hardware registers
Guest-host cooperation protocol for efficient nested virtualization support

metrics.speedup: 1.58x page walk speedup (1.65x with THP), 1.20x application execution speedup (1.14x with THP)
